case_analysis.focal_point: Whether NEPA requires the Surface Transportation Board, when approving a rail line, to analyze environmental effects of upstream oil drilling and downstream refining/consumption allegedly enabled by the rail line as “reasonably foreseeable” indirect effects.
case_analysis.legal_provision: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 4321–4370h (particularly the requirement for an Environmental Impact Statement analyzing environmental impacts), and implementing NEPA causation/foreseeability principles as applied by federal agencies (here, the Surface Transportation Board).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue the D.C. Circuit imposed an unlawfully expansive NEPA standard by requiring the Board to evaluate remote, third-party, market-driven effects (such as increased oil production in the Uinta Basin and increased refining and end-use emissions elsewhere) that the Board does not control and that are not caused by the rail-approval decision in the legally relevant sense. They contend NEPA requires analysis only of effects sufficiently proximate to the agency action—i.e., effects the agency action will cause and that fall within the agency’s regulatory authority—so that NEPA cannot be used as a backdoor to regulate oil development and consumption beyond the Board’s jurisdiction. Amici supporting petitioners emphasize that the lower court’s foreseeability approach is subjective, invites endless litigation, and enables opponents to ‘weaponize’ NEPA to stop infrastructure projects regardless of the agency’s limited authority.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (counties and environmental groups) argue that NEPA requires a full accounting of reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of approving the rail line, including increased oil extraction facilitated by added transportation capacity and the downstream environmental and climate impacts from refining and burning that oil. They maintain these consequences are foreseeable results of the rail project’s purpose and economic function, and that excluding them would improperly segment the analysis and understate the project’s real-world environmental footprint, frustrating NEPA’s information-forcing goals for agency decisionmaking and public disclosure.
key_precedents: Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point that a crude-by-rail line predictably enables increased extraction and combustion is the respondents’ strongest case on foreseeability and NEPA’s information-forcing function, and Justice Jackson is right to warn against segmentation. But Public Citizen supplies a limiting principle of legally relevant causation, not just practical foreseeability: the EIS must remain tethered to effects proximately caused by the Board’s approval and within the realm the agency can meaningfully address, otherwise NEPA becomes a vehicle to litigate and pressure regulation of drilling and end-use consumption that Congress assigned elsewhere. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces my minimalist approach—require a hard look at construction, operation, and reasonably predictable rail-traffic consequences (including safety and local pollution along the corridor), while rejecting any categorical mandate to quantify remote upstream/downstream market activity beyond the Board’s authority. That narrower, precedent-grounded holding respects NEPA’s purpose without collapsing the proximate-cause boundary into but-for causation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s foreseeability/segmentation point has intuitive appeal because this line is designed to move crude, but NEPA’s text still cabins the inquiry to the environmental impact of the “proposed action,” not every predictable market consequence downstream of private choices. Public Citizen’s “reasonably close causal relationship” supplies a proximate-cause limit that Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch correctly tie to administrability and to the agency’s legally relevant authority; otherwise the Board’s approval power becomes a trigger to analyze (and implicitly arbitrate) drilling and end-use emissions Congress placed beyond the Board’s remit. Justice Jackson’s attempt to distinguish Public Citizen on “discretion” does not overcome that NEPA cannot convert mere power to approve/deny into legal causation for third-party production and consumption decisions mediated by markets. On an original public meaning, requiring upstream/downstream lifecycle analysis would effectively rewrite “proposed action” into a roving mandate to assess the broader oil economy rather than the discrete federal approval and its proximately caused effects.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: because the line is purpose-built to move crude, induced extraction and downstream combustion are predictably connected and disclosure would advance NEPA’s information-forcing function. But under Public Citizen, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, NEPA’s “reasonably close causal relationship” is not satisfied by market-mediated but-for foreseeability when the causal chain turns on independent third-party decisions the agency lacks authority to regulate or meaningfully influence; otherwise the Board’s mere approve/deny power becomes a lever to force analysis (and litigation) about the entire oil economy. The “rule of reason” cannot substitute for a jurisdiction- and proximate-cause boundary without collapsing into ad hoc line-drawing and inviting boundless challenges whenever a project has an economic purpose with downstream consequences. I therefore remain persuaded that NEPA review must cover construction/operation and directly induced rail-traffic effects, but not upstream drilling and downstream end-use emissions beyond the Board’s remit.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to press Public Citizen’s “reasonably close causal relationship” limit and the need for administrable boundaries tied to agency authority, but they overread that case as a categorical exclusion whenever third parties and markets intervene. Public Citizen turned on the agency’s inability to act on the information at all; here, the STB is exercising discretionary approval over a rail project purpose-built to move crude, so induced production and resulting refining/combustion emissions are not “roving” consequences but the predictable environmental footprint of the very action being authorized. Justice Kagan’s workability concern is answered by NEPA’s rule-of-reason—requiring reasonable, evidence-based estimation keyed to the project’s designed capacity and likely usage—rather than by segmenting out the most consequential effects simply because they occur upstream/downstream. As Justice Jackson emphasizes, excluding these effects risks underdisclosure and unfairness to corridor communities by understating the project’s real-world impacts, undermining NEPA’s information-forcing function without a sound textual or precedential necessity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s anti-segmentation point has bite—this line is built to move crude, so some induced-traffic consequences are not “remote” and must be analyzed—but her reading effectively turns purpose-plus-foreseeability into a general lifecycle mandate. Under Public Citizen’s “reasonably close causal relationship” limit (as Chief Justice Roberts frames it), the relevant question is not whether oil production/combustion might increase “but for” this approval, but whether those effects are proximately attributable to the Board’s action in light of the Board’s legally relevant authority; market-mediated third-party drilling and end-use decisions are too attenuated to be treated as effects of the “proposed agency action,” especially given the Fiscal Responsibility Act’s tethering language. I would require a robust hard look at construction/operation impacts and reasonably predictable rail-traffic risks (including spill, safety, local pollution), while rejecting an obligation to quantify upstream extraction and downstream combustion emissions that the Board cannot meaningfully regulate without collapsing NEPA into an unadministrable roving inquiry. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on NEPA’s information-forcing function does not overcome that textual and workability boundary, because the statute’s disclosure duty still depends on a coherent causation/authority link rather than an open-ended foreseeability standard.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson offer the best objection: this line is purpose-built to move crude, so induced extraction and downstream combustion are foreseeable and excluding them risks “segmentation.” But NEPA’s text still ties the EIS to the environmental effects of the “proposed action,” and Public Citizen supplies the controlling boundary: foreseeability in a but-for sense does not suffice without a reasonably close, legally attributable causal relationship to the agency action. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, treating the Board’s general power to approve/deny as enough to require lifecycle accounting of market-mediated drilling and end-use would collapse Public Citizen’s proximate-cause limit, convert NEPA into a roving mandate, and press the Board into policymaking Congress did not assign. The Board must take a hard look at construction and operational impacts and directly induced rail-traffic consequences, but upstream and downstream emissions remain too attenuated and governed by independent actors under separate regimes to be NEPA-relevant effects of this approval.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best case that upstream drilling and downstream combustion are foreseeably connected to a crude-oil rail line and that NEPA’s information-forcing purpose is served by disclosure. But Public Citizen’s limiting principle is not mere foreseeability; it requires a reasonably close causal relationship in a proximate-cause sense and asks whether the agency has statutory authority to prevent or meaningfully influence the asserted effect, and here those market-mediated production and end-use decisions remain governed by independent actors and separate regulatory regimes. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, accepting respondents’ “project purpose” theory would effectively deputize the STB to assess nationwide oil-development and consumption impacts as a condition of rail approval—an administrability and institutional-legitimacy problem inconsistent with NEPA’s rule of reason. I would still require a hard look at environmental effects proximately caused by construction and operation (including predictable rail-traffic and safety consequences), while rejecting the D.C. Circuit’s open-ended induced-demand approach.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that a crude-oil rail line predictably induces more extraction and combustion and that NEPA’s information-forcing function counsels disclosure—has force as a policy matter, but it does not overcome Public Citizen’s requirement of a “reasonably close causal relationship” between the agency action and the effect. As Justice Kagan notes, the post–Fiscal Responsibility Act focus on effects of the “proposed agency action” reinforces that NEPA review must stay tethered to what the Board is legally responsible for causing, not to market-mediated third-party decisions the Board cannot regulate (drilling, refining, end-use combustion). Justice Jackson’s attempt to distinguish Public Citizen on the ground that the agency here has discretion to approve/deny still collapses the causation limit into a mere “ability to say no” test, effectively deputizing the Board to inventory (and thereby pressure) nationwide oil-production and consumption consequences beyond its statutory remit. On an originalist/textualist account of § 4332(2)(C), the “proposed action” is the rail approval and its proximately caused construction/operation impacts, including directly induced rail-traffic effects, but not attenuated upstream/downstream emissions driven by independent actors.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan present the best opposing point: Public Citizen supplies a proximate-cause boundary and warns against converting NEPA into a roving inquiry into third-party markets the agency cannot regulate. But that reading overextends Public Citizen’s rationale, which turned on the agency’s lack of discretion to act on the information at all; here, the Board is exercising discretionary approval over a project designed to expand crude-oil transport capacity, making induced extraction and downstream combustion reasonably foreseeable effects of the proposed action under NEPA’s rule of reason. Justice Kagan’s administrability concerns can be addressed by requiring analysis tethered to record evidence and the project’s designed capacity and expected usage, rather than a categorical exclusion of upstream/downstream impacts that risks the very segmentation NEPA is meant to prevent. Because the information-forcing function is about fair, accurate disclosure to affected communities and decisionmakers, I do not think “separate actors and regimes” (as Justice Gorsuch frames it) justifies treating these consequences as legally irrelevant when the approval is a but-for and enabling step for the environmental chain this project is built to facilitate.

John Roberts.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), is bounded by principles of causation and the agency’s statutory authority, and we have rejected environmental review obligations that rest on effects the agency has no ability to prevent or meaningfully influence. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), where the Surface Transportation Board lacks regulatory authority over third-party oil drilling decisions and downstream refining/consumption, those market-driven upstream and downstream impacts are too attenuated to be treated as legally relevant “indirect effects” of the rail-approval decision. A contrary rule risks converting NEPA from an information-forcing statute into a roving mandate to evaluate—and effectively veto—activities outside the Board’s jurisdiction, inviting indeterminate litigation and undermining predictable, institutionally legitimate decisionmaking. The appropriate course is a narrower holding: require analysis of effects proximately caused by the rail line itself, while setting aside the D.C. Circuit’s requirement to assess remote upstream/downstream consequences beyond the Board’s control.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: NEPA’s text requires an Environmental Impact Statement for the “environmental impact” of the “proposed action,” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), which at most reaches effects bearing a reasonably close causal relationship to the agency’s approval decision rather than attenuated, market-mediated consequences of third-party drilling, refining, and consumption. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 767, 770 (2004), mere “but for” causation is insufficient and an agency need not analyze effects it has no statutory authority to prevent or control, even if it could theoretically deny the project altogether. Requiring the Surface Transportation Board to assess upstream and downstream oil-development and end-use emissions would convert NEPA from a procedural disclosure statute into a roving mandate to evaluate (and effectively regulate) activities beyond the Board’s limited jurisdiction, contrary to the statute’s original public meaning and the rule-of-reason limits this Court has enforced. The D.C. Circuit’s expansive foreseeability approach is irreconcilable with Public Citizen’s proximate-cause boundary and would invite unbounded analysis untethered to the agency action.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), does not extend to environmental effects for which the agency is not the legally relevant cause, particularly where the effects depend on independent third-party decisions and market forces. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), an agency need not analyze effects it lacks authority to prevent or meaningfully influence, because NEPA’s information-forcing purpose cannot justify compelled analysis untethered to the agency’s statutory discretion. The Board’s approval of a rail line is too remote from upstream drilling and downstream refining/consumption decisions to make those impacts “reasonably foreseeable” indirect effects in the proximate-cause sense required by Public Citizen. Adopting the D.C. Circuit’s expansive foreseeability approach would have severe practical consequences—inviting endless litigation and turning NEPA into a tool to block infrastructure by forcing agencies to speculate about far-removed economic activity beyond their jurisdiction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: NEPA’s core “information-forcing” mandate requires an EIS to address reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of the action, and a rail-line approval whose purpose and economic function is to move crude oil makes increased drilling and downstream refining/combustion impacts foreseeable consequences that should not be artificially segmented. Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), limits NEPA analysis where the agency is not a legally relevant cause because it lacks authority to prevent the effect, but it does not permit an agency to ignore predictable environmental consequences that flow from the very project it authorizes and that inform the public and decisionmaker about the project’s real footprint. The Board’s limited jurisdiction does not eliminate its duty under 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C) to take a “hard look” at indirect effects it can reasonably foresee, particularly where communities along the route and other vulnerable populations bear localized pollution and safety risks while climate harms are distributed broadly. Requiring disclosure of these impacts promotes fairness and democratic accountability without itself “regulating” upstream or downstream activity beyond the Board’s authority.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS duty, as amended in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, is tethered to the “reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action,” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C)(i), and the statute’s workability depends on a limiting principle that prevents agencies from becoming roving regulators of third-party markets. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, NEPA requires a “reasonably close causal relationship” and rejects mere “but for” causation; where the agency lacks authority over the relevant upstream drilling and downstream refining/consumption decisions, those effects are not legally attributable to the Board’s rail-line approval in the NEPA sense. The D.C. Circuit’s approach—treating the Board’s ability to deny the project as enough to make it responsible for all foreseeable market-driven consequences—risks unbounded analysis, incoherent allocations of responsibility across agencies, and undermines administrable statutory coherence. The better middle ground is to require robust analysis of effects proximately caused by the rail project itself (construction/operation and directly induced rail traffic), while excluding remote third-party production and end-use effects the Board cannot regulate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: NEPA’s text requires a “detailed statement” on environmental impacts of the “proposed action,” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), which—under our “rule of reason”—extends only to effects bearing a “reasonably close causal relationship” to the agency action, not mere “but for” consequences driven by independent third parties and markets. Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen holds that where an agency lacks legally relevant authority over an effect, it need not analyze it; the Board’s approval of a rail line does not make it the proximate cause of upstream drilling decisions or downstream refining and end-use emissions occurring under separate regulatory regimes. Allowing NEPA to compel analysis of such remote effects would effectively turn the Board into a roving regulator of oil production and consumption, contrary to separation-of-powers principles and Congress’s allocation of authority. The D.C. Circuit’s approach—treating the Board’s power to deny a project as enough to require analysis of any foreseeable consequence—collapses Public Citizen’s causation limit and invites boundless NEPA liability untethered to statutory text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: NEPA’s “rule of reason” requires agencies to assess only those environmental effects that bear a “reasonably close causal relationship” to the federal action, and it rejects mere “but for” causation as a trigger for analysis. Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), holds that where an agency lacks authority to prevent or meaningfully influence an effect, NEPA does not require the agency to analyze that effect; the D.C. Circuit’s approach risks converting NEPA into a vehicle to force the Surface Transportation Board to evaluate and effectively regulate upstream drilling and downstream refining/consumption beyond its traditional remit. History, tradition, and workability counsel against an open-ended foreseeability standard that invites speculation about third-party market responses and undermines predictable permitting. Applying Public Citizen, the Board’s EIS need not encompass remote upstream and downstream effects that are not proximately caused by the rail-approval decision in the legally relevant sense.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: NEPA’s text requires an EIS for the environmental impact of the “proposed action,” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), which in this context is the Surface Transportation Board’s approval of a rail line, not upstream drilling decisions or downstream refining and end-use choices made by third parties. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), NEPA does not obligate an agency to analyze effects for which it is not the legally relevant cause—particularly where the agency lacks discretion to prevent those effects—because the information-forcing function is not meaningfully served. The asserted drilling and consumption effects depend on independent market actors and regulatory regimes beyond the Board’s jurisdiction, rendering them too attenuated to treat as “reasonably foreseeable” indirect effects of the Board’s approval in the Public Citizen sense. Precedent and methodological consistency thus counsel rejecting an expansive foreseeability test that effectively makes the Board responsible for environmental consequences it cannot control.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: NEPA’s “rule of reason” requires an EIS to address reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of the agency action, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), and here the rail line’s core economic function is to move Uinta Basin oil—making increased extraction enabled by added transportation capacity, and the resulting downstream refining/combustion emissions, foreseeable consequences that inform the public and the Board’s decisionmaking. Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), limits NEPA analysis where the agency has no discretion to act on the information, but it does not create a categorical exemption for market-mediated, third-party effects when the project is designed to facilitate that very activity and the agency is exercising approval discretion. Requiring disclosure of these effects advances procedural fairness and prevents segmentation that would understate real-world environmental impacts, while still allowing the Board to cabin the analysis to effects that are reasonably foreseeable rather than speculative. On this record, excluding upstream and downstream impacts would frustrate NEPA’s information-forcing purpose and impair informed participation and accountability.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether NEPA requires the Surface Transportation Board (or the reviewing agency) to analyze and disclose environmental impacts from downstream oil-and-gas development and usage that may result from approving a Utah railway project, even when those impacts are outside the agency’s regulatory control and depend on independent third-party actions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 4321–4370h (particularly the EIS requirement and causation/“effects” analysis as implemented through NEPA regulations).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the D.C. Circuit expanded NEPA beyond its proper limits by requiring an environmental impact statement to analyze speculative, attenuated downstream effects (e.g., increased oil production, refining, and ultimate greenhouse-gas emissions) that are not proximately caused by the rail-approval decision and are driven by separate market forces and independent third-party conduct. They contend NEPA’s 'hard look' obligation is bounded by causation principles (including foreseeability and legal relevance), and that under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen an agency need not analyze effects it has no statutory authority to prevent. Petitioners and supporting amici further argue the ruling invites limitless analysis, empowers opponents to delay projects through litigation over ever-more-remote impacts, and turns NEPA into a tool for stopping infrastructure rather than informing agency decisionmaking.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that NEPA requires a full accounting of reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of the federal action, and that approving a major rail line intended to move Uinta Basin oil makes increased extraction, transportation, refining, and resulting emissions foreseeable consequences that must be disclosed to the public and considered by the agency. They maintain that NEPA is an information-forcing statute, and that the agency’s limited authority to regulate downstream conduct does not eliminate the duty to analyze reasonably foreseeable environmental consequences of the approval decision. On their view, failing to analyze these effects improperly segments the action and understates the project’s true environmental footprint.
key_precedents: Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s segmentation point has force: a purpose-built oil rail line predictably facilitates more production and combustion, and NEPA cannot be satisfied by drawing an artificial circle at the edge of an agency’s usual focus. But Public Citizen supplies the limiting principle Justice Kagan emphasizes—NEPA’s “rule of reason” turns on legally relevant causation tied to the agency’s statutory authority, not foreseeability alone—because disclosure that cannot inform any permissible agency choice risks turning NEPA into an unadministrable roving inquiry into market-mediated downstream activity. Here, the STB’s approval may be a but-for condition for the line, yet the asserted upstream and downstream emissions depend on independent producer, refiner, consumer, and other-regulator decisions outside the Board’s control; treating the Board as the legal cause of all that would effectively erase Public Citizen’s proximate-cause constraint. A narrow opinion can still require a robust EIS on construction/operations, spill risk, local air quality, and any indirect effects the Board can meaningfully address, while holding that these attenuated, independently determined lifecycle emissions fall outside NEPA’s required scope for this agency action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that a purpose-built oil rail line will predictably increase production and combustion, and that denying those downstream effects risks NEPA “segmentation.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, NEPA’s text ties the EIS to the “environmental impact” of the federal “action,” and Public Citizen supplies a causation limit requiring a reasonably close—i.e., proximate—relationship grounded in the agency’s statutory authority, not mere foreseeability or but-for causation. Justice Jackson’s attempt to distinguish Public Citizen by emphasizing STB discretion does not cure the core defect: the asserted emissions arise from independent extraction, refining, and end-use decisions outside the Board’s regulatory remit, so the information would not meaningfully inform a choice Congress assigned the Board to make. Under an original public-meaning, text-and-structure approach, treating the Board’s approval power as a hook for lifecycle emissions would erase Public Citizen’s constraint and convert NEPA into an unbounded mandate to analyze remote market-mediated effects.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that this line is purpose-built for Uinta Basin oil, so increased extraction and end-use emissions are foreseeably connected and omitting them risks a misleadingly narrow EIS. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Public Citizen makes statutory discretion and a reasonably close causal relationship the limiting principles; otherwise NEPA’s “rule of reason” collapses into boundless but-for causation whenever a federal approval predictably facilitates private activity. The STB’s binary power to approve or deny the rail line does not make it the legally relevant cause of market-driven drilling, refining, and combustion decisions governed by separate actors and regimes, and forcing the agency to model those effects would not meaningfully inform a decision the statute does not empower it to calibrate. Justice Jackson’s attempt to distinguish Public Citizen on the ground of “meaningful discretion” still fails because it would convert any discretionary permit into an obligation to analyze all foreseeable downstream emissions, an administratively unworkable rule inconsistent with NEPA’s text and our proximate-cause precedents.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to press administrability under Public Citizen and to warn against turning NEPA into boundless but-for causation untethered to agency authority. But Public Citizen’s limiting principle fits best where the agency truly lacks discretion to affect the relevant outcome; here the STB’s approval is the indispensable federal authorization for a purpose-built oil rail line, so increased production and resulting emissions are not a remote market ripple but the project’s reasonably foreseeable, central indirect effects. The Board’s inability to regulate drilling or combustion does not make the effects legally irrelevant under NEPA’s rule-of-reason “hard look,” because disclosure still meaningfully informs the binary approval/conditioning decision and prevents the kind of jurisdictional “segmentation” that would systematically understate burdens on communities least able to avoid them. I agree with Justice Thomas that foreseeability alone is not enough, but when the federal action is designed to facilitate the very activity producing the harm, the causal relationship is reasonably close even if third parties execute the subsequent steps.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s segmentation concern is serious: an EIS that omits the project’s obvious economic purpose can mislead the public about the project’s real-world footprint. But under Public Citizen’s rule-of-reason/proximate-cause framing—emphasized by the Chief and Justice Kavanaugh—the limiting principle is not mere foreseeability; it is whether the asserted effects are legally attributable to the agency action in a way that the agency can meaningfully use in its decisionmaking within its statutory remit. Here, upstream extraction and downstream end-use emissions depend on independent third-party choices and separate regulatory regimes, and treating the STB’s binary approval as making it responsible for all such consequences would collapse the causation limit into boundless but-for analysis and produce an unworkable, incoherent NEPA duty. I would still insist (to meet Sotomayor’s fair “non-misleading picture” point) on a robust analysis of construction/operation impacts and any indirect effects sufficiently tethered to rail operations that the Board can condition or mitigate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press that this line is purpose-built for Uinta Basin oil, making increased production and emissions foreseeable and central to NEPA’s information-forcing role. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas underscore, Public Citizen requires more than foreseeability: it demands a reasonably close causal relationship tied to the agency’s statutory authority, and the STB lacks regulatory control over extraction, refining, or end-use decisions by independent market actors. Treating the Board’s binary approval power as sufficient “legal relevance” for all downstream lifecycle emissions would collapse proximate-cause limits into boundless but-for causation and effectively convert NEPA into a roving mandate to model remote, separately regulated conduct. A faithful, text-bound approach still obliges rigorous analysis of construction and rail-operation impacts (including spill risk and local pollution) and any indirect effects the Board can meaningfully influence through conditions, but not the full downstream market-mediated emissions chain.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: because the line is purpose-built to move Uinta Basin oil, increased production and combustion emissions are plainly foreseeable and excluding them can make the EIS feel artificially narrow. But under Public Citizen’s rule-of-reason limit, foreseeability is not enough; the key is legally relevant causation tied to the agency’s statutory authority, and the STB does not regulate extraction, refining, or end use, which depend on independent actors and separate regimes—so the information would not meaningfully inform a decision the Board is empowered to make. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, treating the Board’s binary approval power as sufficient to attribute all downstream market-mediated emissions would collapse proximate-cause constraints into unbounded but-for causation and make NEPA administratively unworkable. I would hold the EIS must robustly address construction/operation impacts and any indirect effects within the Board’s meaningful influence, but not lifecycle emissions beyond its regulatory remit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly emphasize that the line is purpose-built for oil and that increased extraction and emissions are foreseeable, so an EIS that ignored all downstream effects could risk misleading segmentation. But under NEPA’s text—focusing on the environmental impact of the “major Federal action”—and Public Citizen’s rule-of-reason limit, foreseeability does not suffice without a reasonably close causal relationship grounded in legal relevance; as Chief Justice Roberts notes, the agency’s lack of statutory authority over the downstream conduct defeats attribution even where predictability exists. Here, the STB regulates rail construction and operations, not drilling, refining, or end-use, and requiring lifecycle emissions analysis would collapse proximate-cause limits into boundless but-for causation whenever a project predictably facilitates third-party activity. I would hold that the Board must take a hard look at construction/operation impacts and any indirect effects it can meaningfully influence, but not market-mediated upstream/downstream emissions outside its regulatory remit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability concern under Public Citizen is serious, and I agree NEPA cannot devolve into boundless modeling of every market-mediated consequence. But I read Public Citizen, as Justice Sotomayor stresses, to hinge on the agency’s inability to affect the relevant conduct at all; here, the STB’s authorization is the indispensable federal action for a purpose-built oil line, so the increased extraction/combustion emissions are not “remote” but a foreseeable, central consequence of the approval. Justice Thomas is right that but-for causation is insufficient, yet the causal chain here is tightened by the project’s design and economic function—omitting those effects risks a misleading EIS and the kind of jurisdictional segmentation NEPA’s procedural fairness aims to prevent. The rule-of-reason limit can be honored by allowing qualitative treatment and transparent uncertainty, rather than a categorical exclusion whenever independent actors contribute downstream.

John Roberts.reasoning: NEPA requires an EIS to address the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), but that duty is bounded by a rule-of-reason causation inquiry. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 770 (2004), where an agency lacks statutory authority to prevent or regulate the relevant downstream conduct, it is not a legally relevant cause of those effects and need not analyze them as part of its NEPA review. The D.C. Circuit’s approach—requiring analysis of emissions and development driven by independent third-party and market decisions beyond the Board’s control—risks converting NEPA into an open-ended mandate untethered to the agency’s decision and undermines administrability and institutional legitimacy. A narrower disposition respecting Public Citizen and limiting review to effects proximately connected to the rail-approval decision best accords with precedent and NEPA’s information-forcing function.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: NEPA’s text requires an EIS only for the “environmental impact” of the agency’s proposed action, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), which—under the statute’s original public meaning and this Court’s “rule of reason”—extends only to effects bearing a reasonably close causal relationship to the federal approval. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 767, 770 (2004), an agency need not analyze effects it has no statutory authority to prevent and for which it is not the legally relevant cause; downstream oil-and-gas extraction, refining, and end-use emissions depend on independent third-party decisions and market forces beyond the Board’s regulatory control. Treating the Board’s bare power to deny the rail project as sufficient to make it responsible for all downstream emissions collapses Public Citizen’s causation limit and converts NEPA from an informational statute into a roving license to demand analysis of remote, speculative consequences. Because the challenged downstream impacts are at most “but for” effects and not proximately caused by the approval decision, NEPA does not require their analysis or disclosure in the EIS.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS obligation extends only to environmental effects that are sufficiently connected to the agency action to be legally relevant, and it does not compel analysis of impacts the agency cannot prevent or meaningfully address within its statutory authority. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 767–68 (2004), where an agency “lacks discretion” due to limited statutory authority over the relevant downstream conduct, requiring an EIS on those effects does not further NEPA’s information-forcing purpose because the agency cannot act on that information. The D.C. Circuit’s rule would convert NEPA into an open-ended mandate to study speculative, market-driven third-party oil production, refining, and end-use emissions far beyond the STB’s regulatory control, inviting delay and uncertainty in infrastructure approvals contrary to NEPA’s text and practical administration. The proper NEPA inquiry is bounded by proximate-cause principles and the agency’s jurisdictional limits, so the Board was not required to analyze and disclose those downstream oil-and-gas development and usage effects.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS mandate, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), requires a “hard look” at reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of the federal approval, and a rail line purpose-built to transport Uinta Basin oil makes increased extraction, refining, and resulting emissions foreseeable consequences that must be disclosed to ensure informed decisionmaking and public participation. Public Citizen limits NEPA where an agency truly lacks any ability to act on the relevant effect, but it does not permit an agency to understate a project’s real-world environmental footprint by excluding predictable downstream impacts simply because they involve third parties. Where the Board can deny or condition the approval based on environmental costs, it must confront the full consequences of the action it is authorizing rather than segmenting the analysis into an artificially narrow slice. Given NEPA’s information-forcing function and the disproportionate burdens environmental harms place on vulnerable communities, the D.C. Circuit’s requirement of disclosure is consistent with the statute’s rule-of-reason framework.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS duty is governed by a “rule of reason” that ties required analysis to effects that are sufficiently caused by the agency action, not to every downstream consequence that might follow from independent market and third-party decisions. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), when an agency lacks statutory authority to prevent or control the alleged environmental effect, requiring analysis of that effect does not serve NEPA’s information-forcing function and risks unworkable, limitless review. Approving a rail line may make additional oil-related activity foreseeable in some sense, but the causal chain to increased drilling, refining, and end-use emissions depends on separate regulatory regimes and private actors outside the STB’s control, making the D.C. Circuit’s requirement overbroad. A coherent, workable application of NEPA thus limits the EIS to impacts proximately attributable to the rail-approval decision and those the agency can meaningfully consider within its statutory discretion.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: NEPA’s text and the “rule of reason” limit an EIS to effects bearing a “reasonably close causal relationship” to the federal action, not merely effects that are foreseeable in a but-for sense. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 767–770 (2004), where an agency lacks statutory authority to prevent or meaningfully influence downstream conduct, it is not the legally relevant cause and need not analyze those effects. Here, the asserted impacts from increased oil extraction, refining, and ultimate emissions depend on independent third-party decisions and market forces beyond the Board’s regulatory control, so requiring their analysis would untether NEPA from causation and invite boundless, litigation-driven expansion. Respect for separation of powers counsels against converting NEPA’s procedural disclosure mandate into a roving requirement to evaluate consequences of activities Congress has not placed within the agency’s charge.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS obligation is governed by a “rule of reason” and requires analysis only of effects bearing a “reasonably close causal relationship” to the federal action, not merely effects that satisfy but-for causation. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752, 767–770 (2004), where an agency lacks statutory authority to prevent or meaningfully influence a downstream effect, NEPA does not compel the agency to analyze that effect; otherwise NEPA review becomes unbounded and unworkable. The downstream emissions and increased oil-and-gas development here depend on independent third-party and market decisions and fall outside the Surface Transportation Board’s regulatory control over extraction, refining, and end-use, making the D.C. Circuit’s required analysis too attenuated. Respecting precedent and practical administrability, NEPA should not be expanded into an all-purpose vehicle for litigating remote, indirect consequences of infrastructure approvals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: NEPA’s text requires an EIS only for the “environmental impact” of the “major Federal actions” the agency is approving, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), and this Court has long read that obligation through a “rule of reason” limiting analysis to effects with a “reasonably close causal relationship” to the agency action. Under Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, mere but-for causation is insufficient, and where an agency lacks statutory authority over the downstream conduct, it is not a legally relevant cause of those effects and need not analyze them. Here, downstream oil-and-gas development, refining, and ultimate emissions depend on independent third-party decisions and market forces outside the Board’s regulatory control, rendering them too attenuated to be compelled NEPA effects of the rail-approval decision. Requiring otherwise would expand NEPA beyond its textual and precedential limits and collapse proximate-cause constraints into a boundless foreseeability inquiry.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: NEPA’s EIS requirement is an information-forcing mandate that obligates agencies to take a “hard look” at reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of the federal action, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), and approving a rail line purpose-built to transport Uinta Basin oil makes increased extraction, refining, and associated emissions foreseeable consequences that should be disclosed to the public. While Department of Transportation v. Public Citizen, 541 U.S. 752 (2004), limits NEPA analysis where the agency is not a “legally relevant cause,” that principle should not be read to allow an agency to omit major, predictable downstream impacts that are the very point of the approval decision, even if the agency cannot directly regulate all third-party conduct. Procedural fairness and practical consequences favor requiring full disclosure here, because meaningful public participation and non-misleading decisionmaking depend on understanding the project’s real environmental footprint rather than segmenting the analysis at the edge of the agency’s jurisdiction. Accordingly, I would affirm the duty to analyze these reasonably foreseeable downstream effects while allowing the agency to explain uncertainty and avoid speculative quantification where the record does not support it.
